papers.version_note: arXiv 2303.13617 v3, version of 7 December 2024; the text matches the record.
papers.what_it_is: A conceptual physics paper arguing that the Consistent Histories approach supplies the quantum stochastic-process theory needed for a quantum analog of classical DAG-based causation, illustrated with beam-splitter, spin-half, Bell-inequality and quantum-circuit examples, and criticizing Quantum Causal Models.

assertions.value: The authors state that developing a quantum analog of the classical DAG-based theory of causation requires a theory of random or stochastic time development at the microscopic level, where the noncommutation of Hilbert-space projectors cannot be ignored.
quotes: requires a theory of random or stochastic time development at the microscopic level, where the noncommutation of Hilbert-space projectors cannot be ignored

assertions.value: The authors state that the Consistent Histories approach provides such a theory of quantum random time development.
quotes: The Consistent Histories approach provides such a theory.

assertions.value: The authors state that the mathematical description of causes uses probability theory and that causes are a type of statistical correlation.
quotes: The mathematical description of causes uses probability theory; causes are a type of statistical correlation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how it characterizes causes for its own discussion in Sec. I.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Classical Theory of causes is an approach that makes use of directed acyclic graphs, and that it rests on classical stochastic processes, the standard theory of random time development.
quotes: has been developed in an approach which makes use of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs)
Mathematically it is based on classical stochastic processes, the standard theory of random time development.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the classical DAG description the arrows indicate a time ordering from past to future, and that the conditional probabilities together with those of initial events generate the probability distribution for the histories.
quotes: The arrows indicate a time ordering from past to future.
generate the overall probability distribution for the histories that constitute the corresponding stochastic process

assertions.value: The authors state that some previous attempts at quantum causes start from textbook quantum theory, where time development is unitary and deterministic and randomness appears only when the system is subjected to a macroscopic measurement.
quotes: randomness only appears when that system is subjected to a macroscopic measurement

assertions.value: The authors state that radioactive decay occurs in the absence of a detector, and that a detection event is thought to be caused by the earlier random decay.
quotes: Radioactive decay, for example, occurs in the absence of a detector

assertions.value: The authors state that any satisfactory theory of quantum causes needs to deal with situations of the radioactive-decay type if it is to be of interest to other than philosophers.
quotes: Any satisfactory theory of quantum causes needs to deal with situations of this type
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper sets this requirement as the scope its proposed theory must meet.

assertions.value: The authors state that unstable nuclei decay at relatively precise but totally random instants of time, whether or not a measurement apparatus is nearby.
quotes: Unstable nuclei decay at relatively precise, but totally random, instants of time

assertions.value: The authors define a projector as a Hermitian operator equal to its square, and state that it can be understood as the quantum counterpart of a classical indicator function.
quotes: A projector is a Hermitian operator equal to its square
can be understood as the quantum counterpart of an indicator
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition stated in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors state that for projectors the conjunction P and Q is the projector P Q provided P and Q commute, and that if they do not commute the product in either order is not a projector.
quotes: is the projector P Q provided P and Q commute
the product in either order is not a projector
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as the definition of conjunction in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Logic, invented by Birkhoff and von Neumann, is so complicated that it has been of little help in understanding quantum mechanics and resolving its conceptual difficulties.
quotes: Alas, Quantum Logic is so complicated that it has been of little help in understanding quantum mechanics

assertions.value: The authors state that Consistent Histories treats the conjunction of noncommuting projectors as meaningless, and limits quantum reasoning to collections of commuting projectors called frameworks.
quotes: as meaningless in the noncommuting case, so one never has to discuss its meaning
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as part of the definition of the CH approach in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors define a projective decomposition of the identity (PDI) as a collection of mutually orthogonal projectors that sum to the identity operator, the counterpart of a sample space, and state that the corresponding event algebra consists of the projectors that are members of, or sums of members of, the PDI.
quotes: a collection of mutually orthogonal projectors that sum to the identity operator
The corresponding event algebra consists of all the projectors which are members of, or sums of members, of the PDI.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition stated in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors state the single framework rule: any sort of logical reasoning must be carried out using a collection of commuting projectors, and reasoning that makes simultaneous use of noncommuting projectors is invalid.
quotes: Its single framework rule states that any sort of logical reasoning must be carried out using a collection of commuting projectors; reasoning which makes simultaneous use of noncommuting projectors is invalid.
assertions.certainty_reason: The rule is stated as a principle of the CH approach in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors state that any collection of commuting projectors generates a PDI and so a framework, so that the single framework rule is in that sense not very restrictive; what it rules out is classical reasoning where two or more projectors do not commute.
quotes: What is ruled out is the application of classical reasoning to situations in which two or more projectors do not commute

assertions.value: The authors define a history PDI as a collection of orthogonal history projectors that sum to the history identity, a sample space analogous to that of a classical stochastic process.
quotes: A collection of orthogonal history projectors that sum to the history identity
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition stated in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors state that there are more complicated situations for which a history Hilbert space is needed, a construct first pointed out by Isham.
quotes: There are more complicated situations for which one needs to use a history Hilbert space

assertions.value: The authors state that, unlike a classical phase space, a Hilbert space can in some situations offer no unique way to describe a physical system at a particular time, which they call quantum pluricity in contrast to classical unicity.
quotes: might not be a unique way to describe a physical system at a particular time
quantum pluricity in contrast to classical unicity

assertions.value: The authors state that assigning probabilities to histories of a closed system by unitary time development, provided consistency conditions are satisfied, generalizes the usual Born rule beyond measurement outcomes.
quotes: This represents a generalization, not restricted to measurement outcomes, of the usual Born rule.

assertions.value: The authors state that the correct formulation of the consistency conditions is the medium decoherence condition of Gell-Mann and Hartle.
quotes: the correct formulation of these conditions is the medium decoherence condition of Gell-Mann and Hartle

assertions.value: The authors state that Consistent Histories, unlike textbooks, allows under appropriate conditions the assignment of probabilities to microscopic situations in a closed system at intermediate times.
quotes: allows, under appropriate conditions, assigning probabilities to microscopic situations in a closed system at various intermediate times

assertions.value: The authors state that when two consistent frameworks have a common refinement for which the consistency conditions fail, the single framework rule is extended to preclude such combinations for a closed system whose probabilities use the extended Born rule.
quotes: the single framework rule is extended to preclude such combinations if one considers them part of a closed system and wishes to assign probabilities using the extended Born rule
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as an extension of the rule in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors state that a measurement apparatus, as a physical object obeying quantum principles, must be included in an overall closed system to which probabilities are assigned, and that no textbook wavefunction collapse is needed.
quotes: the measurement apparatus itself, a physical object which obeys fundamental quantum principles, must be included in an overall closed system to which probabilities are assigned
There is no need to invoke the textbook notion of wavefunction collapse

assertions.value: The authors state that it is impossible to construct a complete quantum description of a macroscopic apparatus, but that a general approach retrieves the essential aspects of a measurement process, discussed in a cited earlier paper.
quotes: Of course it is impossible to construct a complete quantum description of a macroscopic apparatus
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit itself in Sec. II B.

assertions.value: The authors state, for a photon emerging from a beamsplitter in a superposition of two path wave packets, that over many runs the fraction in which detector Da triggers is approximately the squared magnitude of the coefficient alpha, and that for detector Db is the squared magnitude of beta.
quotes: Given a large number of runs, the fraction in which Da triggers will be approximately |α|2; those in which Db triggers |β|2.
assertions.reader_inference: The squared magnitudes are printed flat in the text layer as |α|2 and |β|2.

assertions.value: The authors describe, as a gedanken experiment, that blocking path a with a macroscopic absorbing object, treated as an intervention, means Da never triggers while the fraction of runs in which Db triggers remains unchanged.
quotes: Da never triggers, while the fraction of runs in which Db triggers remains unchanged

assertions.value: The authors state that blocking, mirror-replacement and timing observations support the idea that a random process occurs at the first beamsplitter, where the photon randomly chooses path a or b and follows it to the detector.
quotes: These observations support the idea that some sort of random process occurs at the ﬁrst beamsplitter

assertions.value: The authors state that explaining the detection pattern by textbook collapse implies a nonlocal effect that seems strange and is hard to reconcile with special relativity.
quotes: Such a nonlocal eﬀect seems strange, and is hard to reconcile with special relativity.

assertions.value: The authors raise the question of whether a nondetection at Da collapses the amplitude onto path b at the instant of nondetection, or whether a later detection by Db retroactively causes an earlier collapse.
quotes: Does such nondetection result in the amplitude collapsing onto path b at the instant of nondetection?

assertions.value: The authors state that decoherence along the a or b path inside a Mach-Zehnder interferometer would eliminate the interference, so it can be excluded if the interferometer is functioning properly.
quotes: Decoherence along the a or b path inside the interferometer would eliminate the interference, so can be excluded if the interferometer is functioning properly.

assertions.value: The authors set up a Mach-Zehnder interferometer in which the beamsplitters are chosen so that the photon always emerges on path c and is detected by Dc, never by Dd.
quotes: Let us suppose that the beamsplitters have been chosen in such a way that the photon always emerges on path c
assertions.certainty_reason: Setup of the gedanken experiment stated in Sec. III A.

assertions.value: The authors state, following Wheeler, that with the second beamsplitter absent the photon detected by Dc was earlier following path a before the crossing point, and likewise path b when detected by Dd.
quotes: Thus one concludes (as did Wheeler) that with BS2 absent the photon detected by Dc was earlier following path a before reaching the crossing point

assertions.value: The authors state that phase-shifter results imply the photon must in some sense have been simultaneously present in both interferometer arms, which seems odd given the earlier reason to believe it was in either the a arm or the b arm after the first beamsplitter.
quotes: Thus the photon must in some sense have been simultaneously present in both arms of the interferometer.
we had good reason to believe the photon was in either the a arm or the b arm after emerging from BS1

assertions.value: The authors state that providing coherent answers to the questions raised by the beamsplitter experiments is what one should expect from an adequate theory of quantum causes.
quotes: Providing coherent answers to questions of this sort is what one should expect from an adequate theory of quantum causes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this as the standard its theory is to meet.

assertions.value: The authors state that the spin-half Hilbert space has no projector that can represent the combination of an Sx value with an Sz value, so the preparer's and the measurer's statements about the intermediate spin cannot both be combined.
quotes: But there is no room in the spin-half Hilbert space, no projector, that can represent the combination
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated flatly with no proof or calculation in the text.

assertions.value: The authors describe two consistent refinements of Alice's history, in which the identity at the intermediate time is replaced by one of two PDIs, Px and Pz, each a pair of orthogonal projectors on the spin states.
quotes: by replacing I at the intermediate time with one of two PDIs
assertions.certainty_reason: Setup of the spin-half example in Sec. III B.

assertions.value: The authors state that, using the extended Born rule with the Px family, the probability of Sx = +1/2 at the intermediate time, conditional on the initial and final states, is one, and zero for Sx = -1/2.
quotes: Using the extended Born rule means that the probability of Sx = +1/2 at the intermediate time, conditional on the initial and
is 1, and zero for Sx = −1/2
assertions.reader_inference: The value is a result stated without a displayed calculation; the stated words give one as 1.

assertions.value: The authors state that using the Pz family at the intermediate time leads to the conclusion that Sz = +1/2 at the intermediate time.
quotes: leads to the conclusion that Sz = +1/2 at the intermediate time
assertions.reader_inference: In the same passage the final outcome is Sz = -1/2 (the history ends in [z-]) and Bob is sure Sz was -1/2 in those runs; for a final z-minus outcome the Pz family gives -1/2 at the intermediate time (history x-plus, z-plus, z-minus has zero amplitude). The printed +1/2 therefore looks like a sign error in version 3; reader's inference, not the paper's statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the single framework rule means the Px and Pz families cannot be combined to give the nonsensical result that Sx and Sz simultaneously have the values in question, for which there is no Hilbert-space projector.
quotes: The single framework rule means that these two families cannot be combined

assertions.value: The authors state that Alice's late choice of measurement does not influence the particle but only alters what she can learn about it by measurement, with a classical analog of measuring shape versus color of a slip of paper.
quotes: but simply alters what she can learn about it by carrying out a measurement

assertions.value: The authors state that the difference from the quantum case is that shape and color can be simultaneously ascribed to the slip of paper, whereas Sx and Sz cannot simultaneously take on values for a spin-half particle.
quotes: whereas Sx and Sz cannot simultaneously take on values in the case of a spin-half particle

assertions.value: The authors state that Alice, to identify the cause of the Sz measurement outcome, must choose to use Pz rather than Px, and that this is a rational choice of the kind made daily in the laboratory.
quotes: Alice, in order to identify the cause of the Sz measurement outcome, must choose to use Pz rather than Px.
There is nothing irrational about this choice

assertions.value: The authors state that a number of details needed for a complete discussion are omitted, including a proper quantum description of the measurement apparatus and its macroscopic outcomes.
quotes: a number of details needed for a complete discussion have been omitted
assertions.certainty_reason: Limit of the spin-half discussion stated in Sec. III B.

assertions.value: The authors state that their theory of quantum causes extends the Classical Theory in a consistent way, paying attention to the fact that pairs of projectors may not commute, and that it requires a consistent formulation of stochastic quantum dynamics.
quotes: This extension requires a consistent formulation of stochastic quantum dynamics

assertions.value: The authors state, following Gell-Mann and Hartle, that distinct macroscopic situations such as pointer positions are represented by projectors on enormous subspaces of the Hilbert space, which commute with each other in an approximation sufficient for practical purposes.
quotes: Distinct macroscopic situations, such as the pointer positions in traditional discussions of measurements, are represented by projectors on enormous subspaces of the underlying Hilbert space

assertions.value: The authors state that the quasiclassical approach is plausible only if obvious exceptions are excluded, giving classical chaos with positive Lyapunov exponents as deviating from quantum theory at small length scales.
quotes: classical chaos with positive Lyapunov exponents will obviously deviate from quantum theory at small length scales
assertions.certainty_reason: Limit of the quasiclassical argument stated in Sec. IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that, although the ideas of Gell-Mann and Hartle seem plausible, they deserve further study.
quotes: It must be admitted that though the ideas in [15] seem plausible, they deserve further study.
assertions.certainty_reason: Open issue stated by the author in Sec. IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that combining these ideas makes it plausible, not proved, that a Quantum Theory of Causes analogous to the Classical Theory can be constructed from a consistent set of quantum principles.
quotes: Combining these ideas makes it plausible that a Quantum Theory of Causes analogous to the Classical Theory can be constructed using a consistent set of quantum principles.

assertions.value: The authors state that, if that is granted, the Classical Theory applied to ordinary physical processes is consistent with, and a special case of, the Quantum Theory.
quotes: it follows that the Classical Theory as applied to ordinary physical processes is consistent with, and in fact a special case of, the Quantum Theory

assertions.value: The authors state that interventions can be used in the Quantum Theory provided additional projectors are not introduced in a way that destroys the consistency of the family of histories, which need not be considered classically.
quotes: provided additional projectors are not introduced in a way that destroys the overall consistency of the family of histories

assertions.value: The authors state that the Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt Bell inequalities are violated by experiments in precisely the way predicted by quantum theory.
quotes: are violated by experiments in precisely the way predicted by quantum theory

assertions.value: The authors state that the single framework rule forbids combining the four incompatible data sets of a Bell experiment in the way used to derive CHSH inequalities, so the resulting inequalities are invalid.
quotes: The single framework rule of CH states that these four data sets cannot be combined in the way routinely used when deriving CHSH inequalities

assertions.value: The authors state that when Alice measures Sz it would be a mistake for her to assume that the particle also possessed a value of Sx that was there though not measured.
quotes: It would be a mistake for her to assume that in this run the spin-half particle also possessed a value of Sx

assertions.value: The authors state that, for a properly calibrated projective measurement, the Sz value revealed by the outcome was the value possessed by the particle just before measurement, an instance of local causality of the sort Bell thought inconsistent with quantum theory.
quotes: the Sz value revealed by the (macroscopic) outcome was the value possessed by the spin-half particle just before the measurement took place
an instance of local causality of the sort that Bell thought inconsistent with quantum theory

assertions.value: The authors state that, using an appropriate family of histories, the observed Bell correlations can be traced backwards in time to a common cause, with no need for wavefunction collapse, and that the order of Alice's and Bob's measurements makes no difference.
quotes: the observed correlations can be traced backwards in time to a common cause
it makes no diﬀerence

assertions.value: The authors state that a large part of the literature on experimental tests of Bell inequalities becomes irrelevant when classical reasoning is abandoned for Hilbert-space quantum mechanics with quantum histories.
quotes: A large part of the vast literature on experimental tests of Bell inequalities becomes irrelevant

assertions.value: The authors state that the Consistent Histories analysis gets rid of nonlocality claims going back to Bell, and that the simplest explanation of why nonlocal influences are never observed is that they do not exist.
quotes: Among other things the CH analysis gets rid of nonlocality claims that go back to Bell
they do not exist, and are hence incapable of carrying information from one place to another

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum circuits used to assign probabilities to future possibilities from initial data can prove inadequate when searching for an earlier quantum cause of a later property or measurement outcome.
quotes: quantum circuits used in this way can prove inadequate when searching for an earlier quantum cause of a later property or measurement outcome

assertions.value: The authors state that Griffiths and Niu pointed out that the final steps of the Shor factorization algorithm can be made more practical by replacing a final measurement on a collection of qubits by prior measurements on individual qubits at succeeding time steps, with later measurements chosen from earlier outcomes.
quotes: a sequence of prior measurements on individual qubits at succeeding time steps

assertions.value: The authors state that in replacing a conceptual tool with a calculation principle, Nielsen and Chuang abandoned the advantages of the former, namely the identification of earlier causes.
quotes: in replacing a conceptual tool with a calculation principle N&C abandoned the advantages of the former

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum dynamics, both unitary and stochastic, is time-reversible at a fundamental level, and that identifying the cause of a later event requires reasoning backwards in time.
quotes: at a fundamental level quantum dynamics, both unitary and stochastic, is time-reversible
Since identifying the cause of a later event requires reasoning backwards in time

assertions.value: The authors state that the intermediate-time nodes in the Bell-test circuit can be omitted when only the end result of the overall unitary is wanted, but that omitting them removes the possibility of using the circuit to identify the causes of the later measurement outcomes.
quotes: the t1 nodes can
simply be omitted and replaced by trivial unitaries
But this removes the possibility of using the circuit to identify the causes at time t1 of the later measurement outcomes.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the entangled initial state, each pair of outcomes can be associated with a prior state of the qubits at the intermediate time, those prior states are not mutually orthogonal, and so the results from the four kinds of experiment cannot be combined because of quantum incompatibility, which resolves the Bell paradox.
quotes: as these prior states are not mutually orthogonal it becomes obvious that the results from the four distinct kinds of experiment cannot be combined because of quantum incompatibility

assertions.value: The authors state that, from the perspective of the present article, the actual problem of the Wood and Spekkens approach was the lack of a proper theory of quantum stochastic processes.
quotes: From the perspective of the present article the actual problem was the lack of a proper theory of quantum stochastic processes

assertions.value: The authors state that the Quantum Causal Models approach fails because it is not based upon a satisfactory theory of quantum random processes.
quotes: The approach to quantum causes known as Quantum Causal Models fails becuase it is not based upon a satisfactory theory of quantum random processes.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper asserts this by argument in Sec. VII and gives no proof or calculation that the QCM approach fails on any specific case.

assertions.value: The authors state that, from a Consistent Histories perspective, a fundamental problem with Quantum Causal Models is that they are built on quantum-circuit thinking that is fundamentally irreversible in time.
quotes: it is built upon the same sort of thinking that in quantum information studies employs quantum circuits in a way that is fundamentally irreversible in time

assertions.value: The authors state that the Quantum Causal Models approach is bound to fail if a proper analysis of quantum causes requires a time-reversible mathematical structure analogous to the classical one.
quotes: It is bound to fail if a proper analysis of quantum causes requires a time-reversible mathematical structure

assertions.value: The authors state that there is no obvious reason why a time-reversible approach cannot analyze the more complicated situations studied from the Quantum Causal Models perspective.
quotes: There is no obvious reason why a time-reversible approach cannot be used to analyze some of the more complicated situations

assertions.value: The authors state that measurements are not a central concept in Consistent Histories, and that the approach therefore has no measurement problem.
quotes: Unlike textbook quantum theory, measurements are not a central concept in the CH approach.
Thus the CH approach has no measurement problem

assertions.value: The authors state that consistent histories provides an immediate way to embed the modern Classical Theory of causation in the quantum domain, with a consistent framework the analog of a classical sample space.
quotes: The use of consistent histories provides an immediate way in which to embed the modern Classical Theory of causation in the quantum domain.

assertions.value: The authors list as an open problem whether a DAG built for a specific family of quantum histories is useful, stating that a DAG can be constructed but it is not obvious that it will be a useful idea.
quotes: but it is not obvious that this will be a useful idea
assertions.certainty_reason: Open problem stated by the author in Sec. VIII.

assertions.value: The authors list as an open problem whether approximately consistent families are good enough, noting that Dowker and Kent pointed out that when violation of consistency conditions is small there is a nearby family satisfying them exactly.
quotes: if the violation of consistency conditions is small there is a
assertions.certainty_reason: Open problem stated by the author in Sec. VIII; the Dowker-Kent result is cited, not proved here.

assertions.value: The authors list as an open problem treating open quantum systems with an environment by history families, hoping to study decoherence and Markovian behavior with less arm waving.
quotes: This approach is worth pursuing in the hope that it will allow things like decoherence and Markovian behavior to be studied
assertions.certainty_reason: Open problem stated by the author in Sec. VIII.

assertions.value: The authors list as an open problem restudying situations examined by Quantum Causal Models with tools compatible with the quantum Hilbert space, which might provide greater clarity.
quotes: studying them using tools compatible with the quantum Hilbert space might provide greater clarity
assertions.certainty_reason: Open problem stated by the author in Sec. VIII.
